STEPBible glosses the first 'amar' (v.1 pos 16) as 'did he say'; I rendered it as a plain perfect inside the snake's question. The serpent speaks of 'God' (Elohim) alone, not 'YHWH Elohim' as the narrator does; I kept both as the Hebrew has them and say so in the commentary. Ibn Ezra and Radak spend long passages on how a snake can speak; I cite only what they say and do not choose between them.
STEPBible renders מי הגיד as 'who did he tell'; I corrected to 'who told you'. The He-interrogative on hamin ('is it from the tree...?') is a rhetorical question, per Rashbam and Radak.
STEPBible glosses נתתה 'you put'; the ordinary sense is 'you gave'. I rendered 'gave' so the repetition נתתה / נתנה is audible; this repetition is the point of the verse.

הִשִּׁיאַנִי: STEPBible has 'deceived me'; the root is נשא (H5377) 'to lift, beguile'. Rashi (via 2 Chr 32:15) and Ibn Ezra gloss it 'misled / enticed'. I render 'deceived me' in the gloss and 'beguiled me' in the literal layer to keep the older English sense of leading astray by words; the five English versions split between 'beguiled', 'tricked' and 'caused to forget' (YLT).

שׁוּף (H7779) occurs twice with the same form-type, so both layers repeat one English verb ('bruise'). The root is rare (also Job 9:17, Ps 139:11) and its sense is disputed: 'strike, crush' (Rashi, Radak) or 'lie in wait / snap at' (an alternate reading via שאף). I keep 'bruise' in the literal layer and use 'strike' in the dramatic, and flag the ambiguity in the commentary. The pronoun הוּא is masculine singular 'he'; the KJV 'it' reflects the Vulgate/LXX tradition's handling of זרע, not the Hebrew pronoun. I make no messianic claim; the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan reading is cited only as a reading.

הֵרֹנֵךְ (H2032) is 'pregnancy', not 'conception' as KJV/ASV. Ibn Ezra treats the nun as an addition, which I do not rely on. תְּשׁוּקָה (H8669) 'desire' appears also in Gen 4:7 and Song 7:11; I did not resolve its sense beyond noting the debate in Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban. The final word בָּךְ: STEPBible lists a synthetic gloss 'over <the> you'; I glossed it 'over you'.

וּלְאָדָם has no article (H0121G, proper name) unlike הָאָדָם elsewhere; I gloss 'and to Adam' and in the dramatic layer simply 'the man' for continuity. The STEPBible morph for וַתֹּאכַל lists '2ms' with a fem. form tag in the table: it is 2ms (you ate). The packet marks the Qere/Ketiv-like '(LA(bh))' on כִּי; I take it as a text-critical siglum and gloss plainly 'for / because'.

אַפֶּיךָ is dual 'nostrils', by extension face. I gloss 'face' (as STEPBible) and discuss nostrils in the note. 'Bread' vs 'food': לֶחֶם is food in general; the literal layer says 'bread' to keep the harvest-to-oven chain, the dramatic layer says 'bread' too, and the commentary explains the wider sense.

Hebrew has a simple imperfect 'we eat'; KJV/ASV 'we may eat' is a modal reading, YLT 'we do eat' is closer. I kept the plain reading in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer carry the sense of permission.

Rashi's explanation that the Torah returns to the naming of Adam is cited only in summary; I did not rely on his claims about the serpent's motive. The etymology חַוָּה ~ חַי is given in the verse itself (כִּי...אֵם כָּל־חָי); Radak's point about the vav/yod spelling is cited as his own claim.

The verse is deliberately broken off after 'and live for ever': the protasis of פֶּן has no apodosis (aposiopesis); v. 23 supplies the action. I keep the literal layer unfinished and mark it with a dash. הָיָה כְּאַחַד מִמֶּנּוּ is read by Rashi (single among the lower beings), Onkelos (alone in the world), Ibn Ezra (God speaking with angels) and Radak (God includes the angels); I translate 'like one of us' and give the readings in the commentary. The gloss for כְּאַחַד: STEPBible morph tags it 'Acfsa' (feminine) but the word is masculine 'one'; I gloss 'like one'. Ibn Ezra's grammatical comment on the vowel of כְּאַחַד is not reproduced.

STEPBible links עֵדֶן to person.eran (Eran, Num 26:36), which is an obvious misidentification: Eden here is the garden's region/place. I flag it for the ontology review; it does not affect the text layers.

וַיַּשְׁכֵּן (Hiphil of שכן) is 'he made dwell / settled', which the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan takes as the glory of the Presence; I only note the root connection to mishkan/shekhinah as my own observation. 'Cherubim' is already plural; KJV 'Cherubims' double-pluralises. The lamed in לגן is read as 'of' (preposition in construct with the previous מקדם), glossed 'of the garden of Eden'. Sources on the identity of the cherubim (Rashi: angels of destruction; Radak: a vision) are cited by name; I did not assert any iconographic claim beyond the general ANE guardian-figure context stated as my own reading.

The woman's 'neither shall ye touch it' has no counterpart in 2:17. Rashi and Radak both say she added it; Radak also offers a gentler reading (a fence out of love). I report both and take no side. STEPBible morph tags 'bo' as H9033 'in it'; I glossed 'it' / 'touch it' since the verb נגע takes ב.

Elohim here (pos 11 'ke-elohim') can be 'like God' or 'like gods/divine beings'. The plural participle yodei ('knowers of') agrees with a plural 'you' only, so it does not decide it; Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'like angels'. I rendered 'like God' in both English layers and kept the ambiguity in the commentary and notes. KJV 'gods' is a defensible choice, not an error.

Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds that the woman saw Samael, the angel of death; this is not in the Hebrew and I mention it only as tradition. The 'also ... with her' (gam ... immah) is read as 'he was present', after Radak (who has the husband elsewhere in the garden) and against the plain implication; I flagged both.

STEPBible glosses חֲגֹרֹת as 'loin coverings'; I kept 'loincloths' in the literal layer to avoid KJV's 'aprons' and to keep the bodily word. 'Leaf of a fig tree' is singular collective (alēh te'ēnāh).

'lə-ruach hayyom' is disputed: 'at the wind/breeze of the day' (evening, cooling) vs. Rashi's west/sunset direction vs. Sforno's 'the will of the day'. I kept the wind-of-the-day reading as the plain sense and gave the others as options. Also disputed: whether mithallēkh modifies the voice (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Ramban) or God. The literal layer keeps the Hebrew ambiguity: 'the sound of YHWH God walking about'. 'ets haggan' is singular for 'trees', as Radak notes.
Rashi's claim that God knew where the man was and asked to open a conversation is traditional and consistent with Radak and Ibn Ezra; I cite it as theirs.

notes.note: Chapter-wide: the text gives no time word between Gen 2:25 and 3:1, so the whole chapter hangs on evt.gen_2.man_speaks_one_flesh with a one-year margin on the first scene (MACRO_ERA). The only hour in the chapter is 'the wind of the day' (3:8), set at late afternoon (BEIN_HAARBAYIM) after Rashi (the west wind toward evening) and Radak (evening). Rashi, citing Sanhedrin 38b, says the sin fell on the tenth hour of the sixth day, i.e. the same day as the creation of man; I do not force that, and leave the day open (12-hour margin on 3:8), but the dry-run dates will show whether the chain lands on day 6.

Words that come true: God's warning at 2:17 ('in the day you eat of it you shall surely die') is not fulfilled in this chapter in any narrated death (the expulsion at 3:23-24 is often read as the 'death', but the text does not say so); the death of Adam is told in Gen 5:5, and the return to dust (3:19) is fulfilled there too, so the Gen 5 session should write FULFILLS_PROPHECY. The enmity of 3:15 and the pain of childbirth (3:16) point to Gen 4 (Cain and Abel; births), whose session should consider those links. The thorns and sweat of 3:17-19 are fulfilled by the toil of Gen 3:23 only in the sense of sending out to till; no link written.
All verses 3:1-24 are covered. The serpent's speech (3:4-5) is not treated as prophecy (it is a claim, contradicted in 3:7-11 only in part).
